newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parliament starts welfare bill debate.
newsitem.headline: French parliament starts welfare bill debate.

text.p: French social affairs minister Jacques Barrot on Tuesday attacked opposition by doctors to efforts to curb high health care costs as the national assembly began debate on a bill to cut the country's welfare deficit.
"The reforms are not a threat to medicine but rather a chance not to be missed," he told the assembly, launching the three-day debate.
Plans to curtail the generous welfare system have aroused strong opposition from the medical profession which says it objects to treating medical spending as an "accounting exercise".

But the legislation setting out plans to reduce social security costs through spending controls and revenue-raising measures is expected to sail through the assembly and the Senate thanks to the ruling centre-right coalition's big majority in both houses.

The debate on the bill marks a first, coming in the wake of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's announcement last year year that he wanted parliament to review the financing of the social security system annually.

The measure aims to cut the welfare deficit in 1997 to 29.7 billion francs from about 51.6 billion francs this year. News reports have said the goal now is to cut the deficit to 12.3 billion in 1998 and achieve a surplus of 7.9 billion in 1999.
The government had aimed for a small surplus in the welfare accounts by 1997 but slow growth and high unemployment dashed those hopes.
The bill would boost excise duties on alcohol by 1.5 percent, increase duties on tobacco by 3.0 percent and reform payroll charges for health care.

While the bill is expected to get smooth passage, there could be calls for some changes. Alcohol producers are complaining they are unfairly singled out by the revenue-raising plans. And some members of UDF, the junior partner in the centre-right coalition, plan to push for a widening of the revenue base for the welfare system.

Earlier this year, the government carried out the second debt write-off in just over two years to lift the burden of paying debt service charges from the social security system and set up a new welfare debt repayment fund to take on the debt.

The move was meant to set the system back on its feet. But sluggish growth which has left unemployment at a record high of 12.6 percent wiped out all the gains from those changes and the government pledged higher taxes and new cost curbs.

The social security system -- which uses mostly payroll charges to fund healthcare pensions and family benefits -- is run separately from the central government budget and has long been the weak link in efforts to cut France's public deficit.
Co-managed by the employers' federation and trade unions, the social security system has defied all government attempts to restore it to balance.

However, the latest health spending figures released on Monday by the Caisse Nationale d'Assurances Maladie (CNAM) just ahead of the debate on the social security bill gave the government some grounds for optimism.

Health spending fell 0.4 percent in September from the previous month and the Caisse said that "the evolution seen over the last four months strongly reduces the risk of overshooting" the government's goal of containing the rise in non-hospital spending to 2.1 percent for the year.
